analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for merging companies to claim their deal will lower costs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies propose a big merger, they often argue the deal will create efficiencies—cost savings that will supposedly benefit consumers—and courts weigh that argument in the merger's favor. This bill would let courts count an efficiency claim only if it is verifiable, could not be achieved without the merger, and would actually promote competition. It would also put the burden of proving those claims on the companies doing the merging, and require companies that settle with antitrust enforcers to report for five years on whether the promised savings ever reached consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and small businesses. By making it harder for merging companies to justify deals with unverifiable promises of cost savings, the bill would strengthen the government's ability to block mergers that reduce competition, which tends to mean fewer price increases and less market concentration.

how_it_helps.text: A court could count a claimed efficiency from a merger only if it could not be achieved without the merger, is verifiable, and would promote competition [S2][S3].
The burden of proving that an efficiency claim offsets a merger's harm to competition would fall on the merging companies, not on antitrust enforcers [S2][S3].

Companies that settle merger challenges with the FTC or Justice Department would have to report annually for five years on whether claimed cost savings and consumer benefits actually materialized and were passed on to consumers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large companies seeking mergers and acquisitions. Deals that are hard to justify on competition grounds would face a higher risk of being blocked or challenged, and settling companies would face new reporting obligations.

drawbacks.text: Requiring proof that efficiencies are merger-specific and verifiable could block some mergers that genuinely would have lowered costs for consumers, since companies would no longer get credit for real but unverifiable savings [S2][S3].
The reporting requirement would add five years of annual compliance paperwork for companies that settle merger cases with the FTC or Justice Department [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill strengthens antitrust enforcement at a time when industries were consolidating, and the main cost falls on companies whose mergers reduce competition. The honest tradeoff is that some efficient mergers would face greater scrutiny or be blocked, but the burden-shifting and reporting requirements are aimed precisely at the problem that merger efficiencies are often promised and rarely verified.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 26, 2018, and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
On May 22, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill had a Democratic sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors and never advanced past committee referral [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies planning mergers are better off: because the bill died, courts continue to weigh efficiency claims on the old, more permissive terms, and merging companies face no new reporting obligations for settlement deals.

industries.industry: Large corporations pursuing mergers and acquisitions
industries.note: The bill would have raised the bar for justifying mergers with efficiency claims and required annual reporting from companies that settle merger cases. Weaker merger enforcement leaves consolidated industries freer to raise prices on consumers.

industries.industry: Antitrust enforcement agencies (FTC and Justice Department)
industries.note: The bill would have shifted the burden of proving efficiency claims onto merging firms and given enforcers data on whether promised savings materialized, making challenges to anticompetitive mergers easier to win.
